group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A previously independent 29-year-old woman with a five-year history of biopsy-proven focal segmental glomerulosclerosis complicated by steadily declining glomerular filtration—she receives thrice-weekly outpatient hemodialysis but underwent her most recent session the afternoon before presentation—was brought to the emergency department by her roommate after awakening late this morning markedly confused and repeatedly asking why the bedroom looked unfamiliar. According to the roommate, the patient had complained of feverish chills, right-sided chest discomfort when taking deep breaths, and a hacking dry cough that turned thick and blood-flecked over the preceding forty-eight hours; she had taken no antipyretics, cough suppressants, inhalers, supplemental oxygen, or over-the-counter decongestants, wanting “to let it run its course.” The roommate denied illicit drug use, accidental ingestions, or carbon-monoxide exposure in the apartment and confirmed that the patient was last in her usual state of alertness the night before while streaming a movie. Past medical records retrieved electronically list only chronic kidney impairment managed by nephrology, secondary renal anemia treated intermittently with darbepoetin, and iron supplementation; there is no documentation of cerebrovascular accidents, chronic liver disorders, malignancies, or cardiac pump failure. She finished a two-year vocational program in graphic design and works remotely, climbing two flights of stairs to her walk-up unit daily without baseline limitation. She quit smoking cigarettes six years ago after a short three-pack-year exposure, takes no alcohol, and denies recreational drug use. Vaccination history notes completion of both pneumococcal series and last autumn’s inactivated influenza dose. Emergency medical services found her sitting on the edge of her bed, skin flushed and hot to touch, mumbling the wrong month, and breathing rapidly with shallow excursions; they established a saline lock but withheld fluids, antipyretics, nebulized medication, or oxygen so that initial vitals would reflect her untreated physiology. On arrival to the resuscitation bay she appeared ill, eyes wandering intermittently, oriented only to self, and following single-step commands sluggishly but purposefully; Glasgow Coma Scale summed to 14, with spontaneous eye opening, confused verbal output, and localizing motor response. Capillary refill was brisk, mucous membranes were dry and sticky, and no peripheral edema was evident around her permanent upper-arm arteriovenous graft site. Pre-intervention vitals documented an oral temperature of 102.4 °F, a thready yet regular radial pulse racing at 134 beats per minute, a non-invasive blood pressure of 98/54 mm Hg confirmed manually, and a markedly elevated respiratory rate of 58 breaths per minute with faint intercostal retractions; pulse oximetry on ambient air at sea-level fluctuated between 93 % and 95 %. Cardiac auscultation revealed a tachycardic S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or pericardial rub. Pulmonary examination showed markedly reduced breath sounds and stony dullness to percussion over the lower half of the right posterior hemithorax, with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles just superior to that zone; the left lung was clear. Abdominal examination demonstrated a soft, mildly distended abdomen with diffuse tenderness to deep palpation but no rebound or guarding; the peritoneal catheter scar from a childhood therapy was well healed. Neurological screening beyond her clouded sensorium showed equal and reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, symmetric facial expression, and 5/5 strength in all extremities. A finger-stick glucose performed before any intravenous flushes registered 170 mg/dL. Peripheral venous blood and an arterial sample from the left radial artery were obtained within ten minutes of triage, prior to any therapy. Laboratory results returned sodium 162 mEq/L, potassium 4.9 mEq/L, chloride 110 mEq/L, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 61 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine of 7.1 mg/dL, values comparable to her routine pre-dialysis measurements except for the pronounced hypernatremia. Complete blood count revealed leukocytes 17.4 × 10⁹/L with 89 % segmented neutrophils, an alarmingly low hematocrit of 22 %, hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, and platelets 238 × 10⁹/L. Arterial blood gas on room air demonstrated a pH of 7.18, PaCO₂ 22 mm Hg, PaO₂ 98 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 8 mEq/L, indicating severe metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation and preserved oxygen tension. Serum lactate was 3.1 mmol/L. High-sensitivity troponin and bedside ultrasound of the inferior vena cava showed no evidence of volume overload or myocardial ischemia. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph performed before any medication revealed dense consolidation involving the right middle and lower lobes accompanied by a large meniscus-shaped opacity blunting the costophrenic angle, consistent with a sizable fluid collection; the cardiac silhouette and mediastinum were unremarkable for age. Electrocardiography obtained simultaneously showed sinus tachycardia at 132 bpm with peaked T waves identical to previous dialysis-unit tracings and no new ischemic changes. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, pleural fluid aspiration kits, an induced sputum sample for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigen assays for common bacterial pathogens, and a multiplex respiratory viral panel were dispatched to the laboratory before antibiotics or dialysis orders were initiated. At the time this note is written, she has received no antimicrobial agents, intravenous crystalloid, antipyretics, vasopressors, bronchodilators, or supplemental oxygen, ensuring that all physiologic observations, imaging findings, and laboratory values above represent her untreated state on presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points at presentation.
- Demographics: Female age 29 gives 29 − 10 = 19. No nursing-home residence: 0.
- Comorbidities: Chronic renal disease adds 10. No malignancy, liver disease, heart failure, or cerebrovascular disease: 0.
- Examination: New confusion adds 20; respiratory rate 58/min (≥30) adds 20; pulse 134/min (≥125) adds 10. Systolic BP 98 mmHg is not <90, and temperature 102.4°F (39.1°C) is neither <35°C nor ≥40°C: 0 for both.
- Laboratory findings: Arterial pH 7.18 (<7.35) adds 30; BUN 61 mg/dL (≥30) adds 20; hematocrit 22% (<30%) adds 10. Sodium 162 mEq/L is not <130, glucose 170 mg/dL is not ≥250, and PaO₂ 98 mmHg is not <60: 0 for each.
- Radiograph: Pleural effusion adds 10.
Total = 19 + 10 + 20 + 20 + 10 + 30 + 20 + 10 + 10 = 149 (risk class V).
Final answer: 149
